title: Doctors Say Healthy Indians Rarely Need Daily Supplements Without Deficiency
excerpt: Reporting what doctors say: supplements fill confirmed gaps such as vitamin D deficiency or B12 in vegetarian diets, but the USPSTF's 84-study review found little or no benefit from routine use in healthy adults — and the multivitamin cancer signal was 0.2 to 1.2 percentage points in absolute terms.
body:
• Doctors quoted in the reporting say supplements are not medicines and are not a substitute for food — a varied diet supplies most nutrients for healthy adults.
  • The USPSTF review of 84 studies (739,803 people) found vitamin D was not significantly linked to lower mortality (OR 0.96) or cardiovascular events (OR 1.00), and multivitamins' cancer signal was small in absolute terms: -0.2% to -1.2%.
  • Groups doctors say may need supplements are specific: confirmed deficiency, pregnancy (folic acid), vegetarian or vegan diets (B12), older adults, restrictive diets and conditions affecting absorption.
  • Before starting a daily stack, the advice reported is testing and medical input first — excess fat-soluble vitamins, iron and calcium carry risks, and supplements can interact with prescription medicines.

Multivitamins, vitamin D, B12, calcium, iron and protein products are now a daily routine for many Indians. Doctors quoted in a new India Today report ask what that stack is treating in a healthy adult eating a varied diet. Their answer, as reported, is that supplements are not medicines, are not a substitute for food, and may add no measurable benefit when there is no deficiency to correct.

A balanced diet of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, pulses, nuts and dairy provides most essential nutrients, plus fibre a pill does not replicate. For healthy adults who eat that way, the experts said, daily supplements may not be necessary.

What the trial evidence actually shows

The strongest check on routine supplementation is the evidence review prepared for the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), which pooled 84 studies covering 739,803 adults without known deficiencies. Its conclusions are best read in absolute, not relative, terms. Multivitamin use was associated with lower odds of any cancer (odds ratio 0.93), but across adequately powered trials the absolute risk difference ranged only from -0.2% to -1.2%. In the largest trial, COSMOS, 4.8% of participants taking a multivitamin developed invasive cancer over a median 3.6 years, against 5.0% on placebo.

For vitamin D — the supplement most discussed in India — the review found no significant association with all-cause mortality (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.91-1.02), composite cardiovascular events (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.95-1.05) or any cancer incidence (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.92-1.03). The reviewers summarised supplementation overall as associated with little or no benefit in preventing cancer, cardiovascular disease and death in healthy adults, with the small multivitamin cancer signal the exception. One finding cut the other way: beta carotene was associated with increased lung cancer risk (OR 1.20) in people at high risk. The India Today report matches that conclusion: research has not consistently shown routine multivitamin use prevents major chronic diseases in healthy adults.

Where doctors say supplements do belong

The reporting is not anti-supplement; it is anti-routine. Vitamin D deficiency remains a genuine concern in India despite abundant sunlight, with indoor work, limited outdoor activity, clothing habits and skin pigmentation all affecting production, and the report says confirmed deficiency may require supplements on medical advice. Vitamin B12 is the other recurring case, because it is found mainly in animal-based foods — milk, dairy, eggs, fish and meat — leaving vegetarians and vegans at higher risk of inadequate intake.

Dietitian Nidhi Sahai, Head of Clinical Dietetics and Nutrition at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Vaishali, makes the same point for protein in separate News18 reporting. The Indian Council of Medical Research recommends about 0.8 to 1 gram of protein per kilogram of body weight for healthy adults, and Sahai said a well-planned diet — dal and legumes, dairy, eggs, soy, nuts and seeds — can meet that for most people not in intense training. She listed protein supplements as useful for athletes, elderly people with poor appetite, post-surgery patients and diagnosed deficiency under supervision, not as a default.

The groups the report names as potentially benefiting are consistent: pregnant women, older adults, people on restrictive diets, people with diagnosed deficiencies and patients whose conditions affect nutrient absorption. Doctors link specific products to specific needs — folic acid in pregnancy, B12 for inadequate intake or absorption, vitamin D for confirmed deficiency — with dose and duration set individually.

The risks of treating supplements as harmless

The report also warns against assuming over-the-counter means risk-free. Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K can accumulate; high-dose vitamin D without supervision can raise calcium levels; excessive iron can cause digestive problems and, in some circumstances, serious complications; and excess calcium may increase kidney-stone risk in susceptible people — a harm the USPSTF review also flagged. Combining products can duplicate nutrients, and some supplements interact with prescription medicines. The closing advice is procedural: base any decision on dietary habits, medical history and tested need, consult a qualified professional first, and treat a balanced diet — with sleep, activity and hydration — as the foundation supplements at most fill gaps in.
